name: tsl::robin_map (Tessil/robin-map)
workload: int64_t keys (identity hash), 15-char and 50-char std::string keys; insert, successful/unsuccessful lookup, and iteration across table sizes up to millions of elements
claimed_speedup: Open-addressing robin-hood design outperforms std::unordered_map on inserts and lookups in Tessil's multi-library shootout charts; no single aggregate multiplier is stated in text, only per-workload graphs
tradeoffs: Open addressing invalidates iterators/pointers on any modification (unlike std::unordered_map); key/value must be swappable and copy/move-constructible; strong exception guarantee only holds under extra conditions
caveats: Benchmark is hosted by the library's own author (Tessil), not a fully independent third party, though it covers many outside libraries (Boost, google::dense_hash_map, QHash, std::unordered_map); exact numeric speedup vs std::unordered_map is only shown in charts, not quoted as text
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch "hash map faster than std::unordered_map benchmark github C++"

name: tsl::hopscotch_map (Tessil/hopscotch-map)
workload: int64_t keys (identity hash), 15-char and 50-char std::string keys; insert, successful/unsuccessful lookup, and iteration across table sizes up to millions of elements (same benchmark suite as tsl::robin_map)
claimed_speedup: README states hopscotch hashing is 'a cache-friendly data structure offering better performances than std::unordered_map in most cases'; shootout charts show wins on insert/lookup while trailing google::dense_hash_map; no single text multiplier is given
tradeoffs: Same iterator/pointer invalidation caveat as robin-map; hopscotch neighborhood bookkeeping adds a little per-bucket memory; the bhopscotch variant trades some speed for O(log n) DoS resistance
caveats: Same shootout page as tsl::robin_map, hosted by the library author rather than a fully independent party; 'in most cases' wording in the README implies known exceptions; no text-quoted multiplier
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch "hash map faster than std::unordered_map benchmark github C++"

name: tsl::ordered_map (Tessil/ordered-map)
workload: Insertion-order-preserving hash map/set benchmarked with the same Tessil shootout suite (int64 and string keys, insert/lookup/iteration)
claimed_speedup: README: 'O(1) average time complexity for lookups with performances similar to std::unordered_map but with faster insertions and reduced memory usage'; lookup speed is described as similar to, not faster than, std::unordered_map
tradeoffs: Higher memory footprint (8 bytes/bucket by default) to preserve insertion order; ordered erase is O(bucket_count) unless using the provided O(1) pop_back()/unordered_erase()
caveats: Speed claim is narrower than the other Tessil maps: only insertion is explicitly claimed faster than std::unordered_map, lookup is only claimed 'similar'
found_via: GitHub: cross-referenced from Tessil/robin-map and Tessil/sparse-map READMEs (same tessil.github.io benchmark ecosystem)

name: emhash (ktprime/emhash: emhash5/6/7/8 + emilib)
workload: 10M random uint64/int64 key insert, find-hit, find-miss, erase, and iterate operations; separate high-load-factor test at 0.999 load factor with 1M+ pre-sized buckets
claimed_speedup: emhash7 vs std::unordered_map (10M ops, AMD 5800H/Windows10/GCC11.3): insert 66.0ms vs 295ms (~4.5x), find-hit 16.9ms vs 33.0ms (~2x), find-miss 18.1ms vs 52.0ms (~2.9x), erase 20.4ms vs 293ms (~14x), iterate 0.74ms vs 62.6ms (~85x)
compiler_and_flags: GCC 11.3 (Windows/MinGW); exact flags for this comparison table not restated, a neighboring benchmark in the same doc uses g++ -O3 -march=native -std=c++17
tradeoffs: Multiple variants (emhash5/6/7/8, emilib1-4) trade iteration speed, erase behavior (tombstones vs none), and memory layout differently; open addressing means no pointer/reference stability; the 0.999 load-factor mode is non-standard behavior most peer libraries don't support
caveats: Numbers are from the project's own benchmark suite (not independently reproduced here); also separately referenced by Martin Ankerl's (2022) and Jackson Allan's independent shootouts, which corroborate emhash's standing but were not used for the exact numbers quoted above
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch "fastest C++ hash map benchmark 2025 open addressing github"

name: ska::flat_hash_map / ska::bytell_hash_map (skarupke/flat_hash_map)
workload: Integer and string keys; 4/32/1024-byte value types; successful/unsuccessful lookups, inserts (with/without reserve), erases, and mixed insert/erase sequences across table sizes from 10 to millions of elements
claimed_speedup: Author claims 'the fastest lookups of any hashtable I could find'; graphs show wins over std::unordered_map from ~10 elements up, though the gap narrows for large (1024-byte) values and for string keys where 'the choice of hashtable doesn't matter much'; no single stated multiplier
compiler_and_flags: GCC, Linux (exact version/flags unstated); Google Benchmark used as the harness
hardware: Unspecified CPU with 6 MiB L3 cache
tradeoffs: No LICENSE file in the repo (BSL-1.0 text only appears in header comments); open addressing gives no pointer/reference stability; author notes the advantage shrinks for large value types and string keys; distributed as 3 raw headers with no CMake/package-manager support
caveats: No reproducible benchmark code is present in the repo itself (only 3 header files, the benchmark harness lives outside it); blog claims are graph-based without a single quoted multiplier; repo has had no commits since 2018 (>7 years, capped at Tier C given the lack of a reproducible, precisely quoted number)
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/skarupke/flat_hash_map, cross-referenced from ktprime/emhash README acknowledgments and Jackson Allan's C/C++ Hash Tables Benchmark

name: google::dense_hash_map (sparsehash/sparsehash)
workload: Financial ticker-symbol string keys; insertion timing, plus two lookup access patterns: iterating a separate key vector (cache-hostile) and repeated single-key lookup, on MSVC
claimed_speedup: Third-party benchmark (MSVC): std::unordered_map inserts faster (3.77ms vs dense_hash_map's 6.97ms); for cache-hostile iterated lookup dense_hash_map is ~6x faster (1.39s vs 8.39s); for repeated single-key lookup dense_hash_map is reported >10,000x faster (285ns vs 3.69s) which looks implausible, see caveats
compiler_and_flags: Recent MSVC, optimizations enabled (exact version/flags unstated)
tradeoffs: Requires reserving a sentinel 'empty key' (and a 'deleted key' if erasing) that can never legally be inserted; 2-4x memory overhead vs data size; API differs from std::unordered_map in these ways
caveats: The >10,000x single-key-lookup number on the cited third-party benchmark looks implausible (likely a compiler optimization/measurement artifact) and is not a fair hashtable comparison; capped at Tier C for this reason. Note std::unordered_map is actually faster at raw insertion in the same benchmark. Google's own repo performance.html data (doc/performance.html) is from 2004 on a Pentium 4 with gcc 2.95.3 and predates std::unordered_map entirely (compares against SGI STL hash_map instead), so it was not used as the primary evidence here
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch "hash map faster than std::unordered_map benchmark github C++" surfaced veeenu/dense_hash_map_benchmarks

name: libcuckoo (cuckoohash_map, efficient/libcuckoo)
workload: Concurrent multi-threaded insert/lookup/mixed workloads on 120M 8-byte-key/8-byte-value pairs (Figure 1, 4-core, 1:1 read:write) and large-scale insert/lookup throughput on a 16-core machine
claimed_speedup: Peer-reviewed (EuroSys'14): on a 16-core machine the design executes 'almost 40 million inserts and more than 70 million lookup operations per second'; Figure 1 (4-core, 120M keys, 1:1 read/write) places it well above the C++11 std::unordered_map bar, though no exact std::unordered_map multiplier is printed as text (only 'up to 2.5x' vs Intel TBB concurrent_hash_map is quoted numerically)
hardware: Intel Core i7-4770 (4-core Haswell) @ 3.4GHz, 32KB L1D / 256KB L2 / 8MB L3, 16GB DDR3 (main experiments); a separate 16-core machine is used for the headline ~40M insert/~70M lookup number
tradeoffs: Adds per-bucket spinlock/version-counter overhead irrelevant for single-threaded use; find() returns via out-parameter rather than iterator; requires locked_table() for safe bulk iteration; mainly wins when there is real concurrent contention, not necessarily in single-threaded use
caveats: The repo's current universal-benchmark harness (tests/universal-benchmark) only wires up LIBCUCKOO as a table type, no std::unordered_map baseline is compiled in; the concrete std::unordered_map comparison instead comes from the EuroSys 2014 paper's Figures 1-2, where the exact multiplier is visual (bar chart) rather than stated as text; the paper's one explicit numeric speedup ('up to 2.5x') is versus Intel TBB, not std::unordered_map
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch "libcuckoo benchmark std::unordered_map throughput NSDI MemC3 concurrent hash table speedup"

name: sparsepp (spp::sparse_hash_map, greg7mdp/sparsepp)
workload: std::pair<uint64_t,uint64_t> entries inserted in random order into an initially empty, non-preallocated container; random insert, random lookup (known-present hits plus a 10%-present-probability miss set), and delete, up to ~70-100M entries
claimed_speedup: Author's write-up (bench.md): random insert throughput is 'as fast as the two std::unordered_map implementations' (g++ and Boost); random lookup is 'faster than all other alternatives, except for dense_hash_map'; delete is 'outperformed only by dense_hash_map' -- i.e. faster than std::unordered_map on lookup and delete, parity on insert
compiler_and_flags: g++ 4.8.4 and Boost 1.55 (for the boost::unordered_map comparison line); optimization flags not explicitly stated
hardware: VirtualBox VM, 5.8GB total RAM / 5.7GB free before benchmarks, Ubuntu (~14.04)
tradeoffs: Slower than google::dense_hash_map on all three operations tested; the author's README now recommends greg7mdp/parallel-hashmap (or gtl) over sparsepp for C++11+ compilers; sparsepp is optimized for low peak memory during resize rather than raw speed
caveats: Results are presented as graph images in bench.md, not a text table, so exact numeric ratios could not be quoted verbatim; benchmark environment is an older VM from roughly 2016; the repo's own README steers users toward parallel-hashmap/gtl instead of sparsepp today
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch "hash map faster than std::unordered_map benchmark github C++" (sparsepp/greg7mdp surfaced via related-library search)
